ETF trading costs: follow the spread and commissions through a complete purchase and sale

Reconcile hypothetical ETF purchase cash and sale proceeds, distinguish a full quote spread from a one-sided cost, and test how fixed commissions affect different order sizes.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 5 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Reconcile one hypothetical ETF purchase and later sale

Interactive planning lab

Purchase cash paid, including entry commissions$10,015
Net gain or loss after assumed trading costs-$30
Midpoint rise needed to break even on this round trip0.30%

An invented ETF quote, not live market data or an execution prediction. Quotes are symmetric around their midpoint: half the full entered spread is paid on each respective side. All units are assumed bought at the entry ask and later sold at the exit bid; each side has the selected number of executed orders at the same respective quote, with sufficient depth and no price impact. Total units are unchanged when order count changes. No distributions, fund expenses, taxes, foreign exchange, partial fills, ticket-fee exceptions or time value of waiting are modeled. Quote midpoint is not NAV or verified fair value; a limit order does not guarantee a fill or eliminate the spread.

The central idea

The ask and bid already incorporate the assumed spread. Reconcile the actual cash paid and received before adding costs, and keep trading costs separate from fund expenses and market returns.

01

Define the quote and its denominator

An ETF’s displayed price is not a complete trading budget. A buyer may face an ask quote, a seller a bid quote, and either may incur a broker commission. Understanding how those pieces fit together helps distinguish a transaction’s cash cost from the investment’s later performance.

This illustration starts with a hypothetical CAD 25 quote midpoint and a full bid–ask spread of 20 basis points of that midpoint. One basis point is 0.01 percentage point, so the full spread is 0.20%. The assumed quotes are symmetric: the ask is CAD 25.025 and the bid is CAD 24.975.

Each side is 10 basis points from the midpoint, rather than 20. The full CAD 0.05 spread separates the ask from the bid. The midpoint is just the average of those two quotes; the calculator does not identify it as NAV, an executable price or independently verified fair value.

02

Reconcile the dollars paid and received

The example buys 400 whole units at the assumed ask and pays a CAD 5 commission. The units cost CAD 10,010 and the total purchase cash is CAD 10,015. At this point, the CAD 10 concession relative to midpoint is already embedded in the executed price.

Suppose the midpoint remains CAD 25 until a later sale, and the full spread remains 20 basis points. Selling 400 units at the assumed bid produces CAD 9,990 before commission. Deducting the CAD 5 exit commission leaves CAD 9,985 of sale cash.

The completed round trip therefore loses CAD 30: CAD 9,985 received less CAD 10,015 paid. The waterfall explains the same result as zero midpoint movement, less CAD 10 of entry spread concession, CAD 10 of exit spread concession and CAD 10 of combined commissions.

Do not deduct another full spread from those cash figures. Buying at the ask and selling at the bid has already included it under these assumptions. A commission is an additional charge; a spread concession is a difference between execution price and the chosen reference quote.

03

Separate proportional costs from fixed ticket charges

The grouped bars compare independent trades of different unit quantities. Spreads remain the same percentage of the respective quote midpoints. At unchanged midpoint, doubling units doubles the dollar spread concession while keeping its share of entry midpoint notional unchanged.

The selected flat commissions behave differently. With one executed order on each side, their combined CAD 10 cost is spread across more units in a larger transaction. The chart expresses both cost components relative to units multiplied by entry midpoint, before commissions, so the denominator is consistent across the bars.

This comparison does not recommend increasing a purchase beyond the financial plan. It isolates a fee schedule’s arithmetic. A smaller suitable purchase and a larger unsuitable purchase cannot be ranked by transaction-cost percentage alone.

The model permits at least 24 whole units and at most 24 executed orders per side. The same total units can therefore be divided into whole-unit orders without requiring fractional-share trading. It assumes each order receives the same respective quote and incurs the selected flat charge.

04

Read more orders as the same capital divided differently

The matrix holds the selected total units fixed while changing the number of executed orders and the spread. Four orders per side do not mean four times as many units or four times the invested capital. They divide the same total quantity into smaller pieces.

At the default 400 units, unchanged midpoint and 20-basis-point spreads, four CAD 5 commissions on entry and four on exit total CAD 40. Spread concessions still total CAD 20, producing a CAD 60 net loss. With a zero commission input, splitting the same quantity adds no modeled commission cost.

Each matrix row replaces both the entry and exit full spreads with its labelled value. Outside the matrix, the controls allow those two spreads to differ. Real prices and depth may change between orders, so neither view predicts what splitting a live order will cost.

05

Solve the movement needed to recover the modeled costs

A small increase in midpoint does not automatically make the completed trade profitable. Under the default assumptions, net sale proceeds equal purchase cash only after the midpoint rises by approximately 0.3003%. The calculation includes both commissions and the exit bid discount from its new midpoint.

That threshold is slightly different from dividing CAD 30 by CAD 10,000, because the exit spread concession also grows with the exit midpoint. The tool solves the cash equality directly rather than treating every cost as a fixed opening-dollar amount.

The final chart varies midpoint movement and displays net gain or loss after the assumed execution costs. It omits fund distributions, management expenses, taxes, foreign exchange and other account charges. It is therefore a narrow trading reconciliation rather than an ETF’s complete holding-period total return.

06

Treat price protection and execution certainty as separate questions

Vanguard Canada’s trading guidance explains that a limit order sets an acceptable execution price but can remain partly or entirely unfilled. It also notes that market conditions and the tradability of underlying holdings can affect ETF spreads.

This calculator assumes a complete fill at the selected ask and bid, with enough quoted depth and no market impact. It does not model a limit order’s fill probability, guarantee that a displayed quote remains available, or assume that a limit order eliminates spread costs.

For an actual transaction, check the current quote, quantity, broker charges and order terms alongside the investment plan. Keep the quote time and denominator visible when comparing spreads. A clear reconciliation of paid and received cash is useful precisely because it leaves the uncertain execution outcome and the separate investment decision open to proper review.
